title: Sacred time (CCC 1163–1173)
hook: Sunday and the year make time holy

segments.voice: Yesterday, words, song and images, and the one who sings prays twice. Your line was sing it. Which line did you sing, and where? Day one thousand ninety-one.

A life can run on several calendars at once. There's work time, with its deadlines. School time, with its terms and breaks. Money time, with its paydays and bills. And sports time, with its seasons and finals. The Catholic Church keeps another calendar running underneath all of those. Its week has a center. Its year has seasons with their own colors. Purple, white, green, red, on the priest's vestments and the cloth on the altar. A family can go a long while without noticing it. The calendar keeps turning anyway, week after week. Today, the Catechism explains what that calendar is for.
screen: `WORK, SCHOOL, MONEY, SPORTS.` → `ANOTHER CALENDAR UNDERNEATH.` → `PURPLE, WHITE, GREEN, RED.`

segments.voice: First, the week has a center: Sunday. The Catechism calls it the Lord's Day, the day Christ rose from the dead. The Apocalypse uses the same name. John writes, in the Douay-Rheims, "I was in the spirit on the Lord's day." The Catechism also calls Sunday both the first day of the week, the day creation began, and the eighth day, a day beyond the ordinary week, a sign of the new creation. It's the day Catholics gather for Mass, a kind of weekly Easter. Second, the year has a heart: Easter. The Catechism calls it the feast of feasts, and quotes Saint Athanasius, who called it the Great Sunday. The Catechism says the light of the Easter days fills the whole year that follows. Third, the year tells the whole story. Around Easter, the Church walks through the life of Christ: waiting for him in Advent, his birth at Christmas, his appearing to the nations, Lent's long walk toward the cross, and the weeks of Easter. Alongside, the Church keeps feasts of Mary and the memories of martyrs and saints, people the Catechism says show Christ's Easter at work in real lives. Fourth, the word today. The Catechism points out that the liturgy keeps saying today: today Christ is born, today he is risen. Not as if it's happening again, but because, Catholics believe, God's saving work isn't trapped in the past. A psalm sung at Easter says it: "This is the day which the Lord hath made: let us be glad and rejoice therein." So sacred time isn't extra time squeezed in on top of ordinary life. In the Catholic view, it's ordinary time, every day of it, given a shape and a center.
screen: `SUNDAY, THE LORD'S DAY.` · `EASTER, THE FEAST OF FEASTS.` · `THE YEAR TELLS THE STORY.` · `THIS IS THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: mark today's season. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself where today sits in the Church's year. Advent, Christmas, Lent, Easter, or the long stretch the Church calls Ordinary Time. If you don't know, that's fine. You can look it up after the bell, or ask someone who goes to Mass. For now, let the question itself slow you down: today is not just a Tuesday or a Friday. It's part of a story with a shape. If you pray, you can offer this day to God as one day of that story. If you don't, simply notice the day you're in, its weather, its light, as a day that won't come again. The bell holds the time.
Sacred time. Sunday, the Lord's Day, at the center of the week, and Easter, the feast of feasts, at the heart of the year, giving every ordinary day a shape. Today's word.
Your line: time made holy. Today, find out the season and its color, and let one thing you see in that color remind you of it. Day one thousand ninety-one.

howItsDone: Catholics gather for Mass on Sundays and holy days, and follow the liturgical year's seasons, Advent, Christmas, Lent, Easter and Ordinary Time, marked by readings and the colors of the priest's vestments.
